claims.text: DFT-derived electronic structure combined with Boltzmann transport can calculate the electronic thermal conductivity separately.
Machine-learned anharmonic force fields can be used to calculate lattice transport and phonon scattering.
The proposed force-field treatment will explicitly capture oxygen-induced defect scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed framework will reduce predictive error by 30–50% relative to Debye-temperature, elastic-property-based, or otherwise conflated models.
The target material is bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen or less.
The target HfNbTaTiZr has mostly ordered local environments.
Below 200 K, the lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions of HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
The framework is applicable from approximately 20 K to 1200 K.
Oxygen impurities induce local lattice distortions and modified bonding environments in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen-induced local distortions and explicit electron-phonon interactions mediate separation of the lattice and electronic heat-transport channels.
Independent calculation of phonon lifetimes and electron relaxation times decouples the lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity channels.
The lattice thermal conductivity will decline gradually at high temperature rather than exhibiting a sharp Debye-type drop.
The separately calculated lattice and electronic contributions will sum to 10–17 W/(K·m) at high temperatures.
The predicted individual lattice and electronic conductivities will match independently separated low-temperature measurements.
Earlier approaches relied on Debye-temperature estimates, DFT-derived elastic properties, or ideal defect-free models.
Earlier approaches conflate lattice and electronic contributions and fail to capture chemical disorder and oxygen-defect effects.
The predictions may not apply above 1 wt.% oxygen or to substantially different microstructures.
Deviation of either separated channel by more than the stated 30–50% margin, or failure of their high-temperature sum to lie within 10–17 W/(K·m), is proposed as a falsification criterion.
